# Overview

This viewer shows, interactively inside Blender, the subject's **real-shape SMPL body mesh** and the
**RGB sensor axes at the 8 IMU locations**, reconstructed from the PRISM
**small / large / anthro** reference data. It is not a video (mp4) but a 3D scene you can
**orbit, play, and scrub**, with two analysis features on top (dataset-run switching and per-IMU
live signal plots).

![The viewer — subject SMPL body + the 8 IMU RGB axes (X=red, Y=green, Z=blue).](figures/viewer_body.png){width=62%}

- **Shape**: an exact mesh built from the subject's own SMPL betas.
- **8 IMU sites** (sensor codes): `back_T4` (upper thoracic back) · `occiput` (back of head) ·
  `wrist_l`·`wrist_r` · `shank_l`·`shank_r` · `foot_l`·`foot_r` (insole).
- **Axis convention**: X=red, Y=green, Z=blue (computer-vision standard frame, `00_sensors.qmd` spec).

# How to run (no installation)

This viewer is **Windows only**.

1. Double-click `launch.exe` in the distribution folder.
2. **No Python, Blender, or add-on needs to be installed** on this PC — Blender, the scripts and the
   plotting library are all inside the folder. The data is read from this PC's bundles, so set
   `SOMA_DATA_ROOT` first (see "Data location and adding runs" below).
3. On first launch the Blender splash appears briefly, then the scene loads.

# Screen and basic controls

In the 3D viewport:

| Action | Key / mouse |
|---|---|
| Play / pause | **Spacebar** |
| Orbit | **middle-mouse drag** |
| Zoom | **mouse wheel** |
| Move frame | drag the timeline below |

All features are controlled from the **`SOMA` panel** on the right. If it is hidden, press **`N`** in the
3D view to open the sidebar and select the `SOMA` tab.

![The SOMA side panel — run selector (count · Reload · Rescan) · IMU plot · display toggles · playback speed · plot update rate.](figures/ui_side_panel.png){width=44%}

# Features

## Dataset run selector

With hundreds or thousands of runs a single list is useless, so the top of the `SOMA` panel narrows
in **three steps**.

| Step | Control | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Collection** dropdown | Runs grouped by dataset and subject (e.g. `prism_faithful_full/prism-subj001 (25)`); the number is how many runs it holds |
| 2 | **Search box** (magnifier) | Keeps only runs whose name contains what you type |
| 3 | **Run** dropdown | Lists only the runs matching both |

Changing the collection re-points the run list and selects its first run, rebuilding the body + IMU
animation (seconds to tens of seconds for the rig). **[Reload run]** rebuilds the current run. If a
collection holds a great many runs the list shows the first 200 and says **"showing N of M"**, so you
can narrow further with the search box — nothing is truncated silently.

**Opening a dropdown re-scans the dataset folder**, so a run copied in while the viewer is running
still shows up. Press **[Rescan dataset]** to look again immediately. The total number of runs found
is shown at the top.

## IMU live plot

Pick an IMU from the **[IMU live plot]** dropdown and its signals show in the adjacent image panel in
**three stacked plots** — from top: **acceleration (m/s²) · angular velocity (deg/s) · orientation
(deg, roll·pitch·yaw)**. The three line colors (red·green·blue) in each plot are the same X·Y·Z axes as
the RGB axes in the 3D view. During playback a **vertical cursor** tracks the current frame.

![IMU live plot — acceleration, angular velocity, orientation (3 panels); the vertical line is the current frame.](figures/imu_plot.png){width=48%}

The dropdown names are the `small_reference.npz` sensor codes directly: `back_T4` (upper thoracic
back) · `occiput` (back of head) · `wrist_l`·`wrist_r` · `shank_l`·`shank_r` · `foot_l`·`foot_r` (insole).

## Display toggles

Two toggles on the **Display** row of the `SOMA` panel keep the view clean.

![Display toggles — show/hide the IMU axes and the joint skeleton.](figures/ui_toggle.png){width=52%}

- **IMU axes** (on by default): show/hide the 8 IMU RGB axes.
- **Skeleton** (off by default): show/hide the SMPL joint skeleton (armature). There is one bone per
  joint (24 total), so it is hidden by default. Hiding it does not affect the mesh deformation.

## Playback speed

The **[Speed (fps)]** slider sets the playback rate. The data is 100 Hz, so **100 = real time** (10 s
total); lower is slower (e.g. 25 → 4× slow motion), higher is faster. The scene is heavy, so if the PC
cannot reach 100 fps the playback slows down — but this viewer uses **frame dropping**, so it skips
frames it cannot draw and **plays at real-time speed**. If it is still slow, lower the Speed for smooth
playback.

## Plot update rate (3D smoothness)

The **[Plot update (Hz)]** slider sets how many times per second the IMU plot is redrawn during
playback (default `20`). Redrawing that plot is the most expensive thing happening during playback, so
**lowering this makes the 3D view smoother.**

| Value | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `20` (default) | 20 redraws/s — the cursor keeps up with playback |
| `30` | the maximum; finest cursor, at the cost of 3D speed |
| `4`–`10` | fewer redraws, 3D gets priority (`4` was the previous default) |
| `1`–`2` | redraws almost never |
| `0` | no redraws during playback (only on pause/scrub) — **smoothest 3D** |

Even at `0` the plot refreshes immediately when you pause or pick a different IMU.

# Data location and adding runs

The viewer carries no data. It reads **the bundles on the PC it runs on**. Bundles stay on the PC
that made them (ADR-0041), and that PC's data root is what the `SOMA_DATA_ROOT` environment variable
names.

```
<SOMA_DATA_ROOT>\
├─ runs\experimental_generation_poc_demo\
│   ├─ <bundle>\                <- the data (e.g. gaitex_unified8, hknu_unified8)
│   │   ├─ INDEX.json           <- list of runs it holds; the viewer reads this to find them fast
│   │   └─ <run-id>\ ...
│   └─ _runs\  _superseded\     <- run records and evidence (the viewer does not walk them)
└─ body_models\smpl\            <- SMPL models (movable with SOMA_BODY_MODEL_DIR)

<deploy folder>\                <- this viewer (where deploy_viewer.ps1 -Dest copied it)
├─ data\SMPL_MALE_clean.npz     <- when the SMPL models are shipped with the viewer
├─ scripts\  blender\  manual\
└─ launch.exe
```

::: {.callout-important}
The viewer does not scan the folders beside itself. To see bundles, set `SOMA_DATA_ROOT`, or name
the folder to look in (item 1 of the scan order below).
:::

When a collection ships an **`INDEX.json`**, the viewer reads that list instead of searching every
folder. With thousands of runs the difference is large — a folder walk takes minutes (longer on a network
drive), while reading the list is near-instant. Collections without one are searched folder by
folder as before.

An entry may name its run folder in **any** of `out_dir`, `relative_path`, `take` or `take_id`; all
four are read, so a catalog written by a different generator still works. If no entry names a folder,
the viewer says so on the console and falls back to searching. The runs found are the same either
way — only slower — so that line is the thing to check if filling the list suddenly takes minutes.

The viewer scans for run folders in this **order** and pools everything it finds into the dropdown
(on a name clash the earlier root wins):

1. a folder named explicitly — the Blender argument `-- --folder <dir>` (repeatable) or the
   `SOMA_VIEWER_DATASET` environment variable
2. `SOMA_DATA_ROOT\runs\experimental_generation_poc_demo\` — **this PC's bundles (the default)**
3. `data\runs\` inside the viewer folder (for a fallback copy)

With neither `SOMA_DATA_ROOT` nor a named folder, the viewer says on the console what to set and
stops. SMPL models are looked for in the viewer's `data\`, then `SOMA_BODY_MODEL_DIR`, else
`SOMA_DATA_ROOT\body_models\smpl`.

**Adding a run**: a bundle `soma-synth run` makes lands under `SOMA_DATA_ROOT` and appears on the next
launch (or when the dropdown is opened). Runs elsewhere are shown by naming their folder as in item 1. A run folder needs `small_reference.npz`, `large_reference.npz`, and an
`anthro_reference.npz` (older bundles: `development_reference.npz`) carrying the shape (`betas`,
`gender`).

**The body is drawn on the model matching the subject's gender.** `betas` live in the shape space of
their own gendered model, so putting a woman's betas on the male template does not approximate her
body — it draws **a different one** (measured ~23 cm apart). The viewer reads `gender` and picks
`SMPL_FEMALE_clean.npz` or `SMPL_MALE_clean.npz`. A deployment carrying only one of them falls back
to it **and says so on the console** — the shape on screen is then not that subject's.

Datasets prefix the joint **rotation** array with their own source name
(`smpl_global_orientation_prism_world`, `smpl_global_orientation_world`, …). The viewer does not
hard-code one name: it takes any `[T,24,4]` array starting with `smpl_global_orientation`, so **any
dataset following the contract opens without a code change**.

It also needs a **root translation** — the trajectory the body follows through the world — and looks
for it in this order:

1. `smpl_trans` in `anthro_reference.npz`
2. `smpl_trans` in `large_reference.npz` — the canonical home once it is published there
3. `smpl_root_translation.npz`, a companion file recovered from the source recording
4. `trans` in a `*_smplx.npz` in the same folder
5. **none of them → the take plays in place**: pose and IMU frames are still exact, only the travel
   through the world is missing

In case 5 the panel shows **"no root translation — playing in place"**. It is never silent.

::: {.callout-warning}
Do **not** assume `pelvis_position_world_aux` is the translation. In AMASS bundles it happens to equal
it; in PRISM ones it is the pelvis **marker** and drifts from the SMPL root by up to ~0.1 m over time.
The same field name means different things per dataset, so
`scripts/poc/enrich_root_translation.py` settles it against each run's source recording and writes
the companion file in step 3.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
Long takes take longer to load: a 10 s take (1,000 frames) is a few seconds, a 2 min take (13,000
frames) about a minute before playback starts, roughly in proportion to the frame count.
:::
